definition: Of work: made entirely by hand and mind, without machine assistance; carried as a quiet mark of provenance, as organic is for food.
etymology: Standard English unprompted (‘without being asked’), re-minted as a label of quality rather than coined afresh. Prompt is Latin promptus, ‘brought forth, ready’, from promere, ‘to take out’. For most of its life the verb lived in the theatre and the schoolroom: the prompter in the wings feeding an actor the line he has dropped, the teacher leaning towards the answer so the pupil will find it. Unprompted was the compliment that came after. The child said thank you unprompted; the witness came forward unprompted. It meant the thing had come from inside the person, with nobody whispering. The word has not moved. What has moved is who does the whispering.
the_case: We already label things this way, just not writing. Honey says whose bees it came from. Pottery says hand-thrown. None of these labels claims better. They claim how, and they exist because the other way of making became the ordinary one. Writing has never needed such a label, because until recently there was only one way to make it. Now there are two, and the obvious candidates all fail: handwritten is too literal, original means nothing any more, human-made sounds like a defence lawyer. Unprompted works because it was already a compliment, and because it points at exactly the act in question: nobody asked a machine. It is the volume’s one deliberate re-minting — the metal centuries old, only the stamp new. Ghostwrought named the work with no hand in it, and handfinish the pass that puts a hand back. This is the far end of that line. The machine can now add almost anything to a page. The one thing it can never add is its own absence.
seo_title: unprompted — work made with no machine anywhere near it
seo_description: Honey says whose bees. Pottery says hand-thrown. Unprompted re-mints an old compliment as a label for work made by hand and mind alone: nobody asked a machine.
